title: DotPy Day 4 narration — fictional training examples
narration: Welcome back to DotPy. Today is Day Four of Excel Intermediate to Master, delivered in Google Sheets. We are going to move from individual calculations to the kind of summary report a chief administrative officer or private secretary might present to management. By the end of this lesson, you will have worked through PivotTables, filtering and slicers, monthly performance measures, charts, an executive dashboard, and final reconciliation. This is a practical class. Keep your Day Four Practical workbook open in a second tab. Pause whenever I demonstrate a step and try it yourself. Our training records are fictional, and the fixed reporting date is the thirtieth of September, twenty twenty-six.

Imagine that management asks two questions. How much did each department spend on approved travel? And are our correspondence and action registers improving over time? A spreadsheet full of rows is not a good answer on its own. You need a summary that groups the right records, measures the right population, and makes exceptions visible. You also need to be able to trace every headline number back to its source. That is our standard today: accurate, readable and explainable. We will demonstrate each step, check the expected result, then practise it again without guessing.

Our exercise covers April through September twenty twenty-six. Travel contains ninety trips. The correspondence register has ninety-six received items. The Actions register has sixty actions. Do not mix those populations. A trip is not a letter, and an action is not a closed letter. Our travel amount is in rand. Other measures are counts or percentages. The Day Four workbook also has Pivot, Monthly, Summary, Dashboard, and Notes sheets. Open the Start sheet first, save a copy using your own learner ID, and leave the source rows untouched. Every example is based on those fictional training records.

A common mistake is to start by clicking Insert, without deciding what we want to know. Start with the management question. For travel, we want expenditure by department and approval status. Department is a category; approval is another category; total cost is a number that can be added. For performance, we want counts grouped by the month an item was first received or raised. These are different calculations. Take ten seconds and say out loud which field identifies the category, which identifies the date, and which field is the measure. Being clear now saves considerable time later.

Now we begin exercise D4 G1. Picture ninety travel rows. You could build several SUMIFS formulas, one for every department and approval category. That would work, but a PivotTable can summarise many categories quickly and make the structure visible. A pivot does not fix errors in its source. If a cost is typed as text, if a department is misspelled, or if a trip is omitted from the source range, the result can be misleading. So inspect the Travel headers and a few sample records before you create it. We are answering: how much recorded and approved travel belongs to each department?

On the Travel sheet, identify columns A through L. A contains the trip identifier; B holds the trip date; D is Department; F is Approval; K is TotalCost; and L holds the first date of the travel month. We need columns D, F and K for our first pivot, but we will select the full source table with headings. Ensure the TotalCost entries are numerical values, not strings beginning with a rand symbol. In a typical sheet, you can use Format, Number, Currency to display an amount as rand without turning its underlying value into text.

Click a cell in the Travel data. Select the full range A1 through L91 if Google Sheets has not detected it correctly. Choose Insert, then Pivot table. Select Existing sheet if that option is offered, and use Pivot A3 as the output location. In the Pivot table editor, add Department to Rows. Add Approval to Columns. Add TotalCost to Values. We are using the Google Sheets menu. Do not hunt for Excel's PivotTable Analyze ribbon: that desktop interface is different. Check that the resulting report has three department rows and separate Approved and Pending columns.

This check is crucial. In the Values setting, the operation should be SUM of TotalCost. Why? Because the question asks how many rand were spent, not how many trips exist. If the editor uses COUNT, the grand total might be ninety; that counts records, not money. Change Summarize by to SUM. The all-status grand total from our answer workbook is three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty rand. The number of trips is ninety. One is currency and the other is a record count. Never use them interchangeably. Format the resulting amounts as rand, preferably without hiding the totals.

Let's read the completed pivot. Executive has approved expenditure of eighty-six thousand seven hundred rand, pending twenty thousand seven hundred, and a total of one hundred and seven thousand four hundred. Finance has approved seventy-six thousand eight hundred and ten, pending thirty thousand three hundred and seventy. Operations has approved seventy-seven thousand one hundred and ninety-five, with twenty-nine thousand seven hundred and sixty-five pending. The three approved amounts total two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five. Pending totals eighty thousand eight hundred and thirty-five. Together they reconcile to the full recorded amount of three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty.

The arithmetic is simple but it is important. Approved plus Pending equals all-status spending, and this should also hold for every department. Executive: eighty-six thousand seven hundred plus twenty thousand seven hundred equals one hundred and seven thousand four hundred. In the total row, two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five plus eighty thousand eight hundred and thirty-five equals three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty. If those do not add up on your pivot, stop. You may have hidden a category, used COUNT rather than SUM, or selected only part of the register. The pivot table is useful because it allows us to verify the components as well as the grand total.

Suppose your pivot displays two versions of the same department: Finance and Finance with an accidental space. They will appear as separate categories. Or suppose TotalCost contains numeric-looking text; the pivot may not aggregate it as expected. Or imagine the source selection stops at row eighty instead of ninety-one. In each case, the table may still look professional while the answer is wrong. The solution is to inspect the underlying register, not to type a corrected number over the pivot. Ask yourself: are we summing the right field, from the right range, with the right categories?

Your first independent check is to build or inspect the same pivot in your own workbook. Confirm the department names, the Approved and Pending column headings, and the grand total. Then answer this question: why can the pivot show a larger amount than Summary B3? The answer is that the pivot grand total includes both approved and pending travel, while Summary B3 includes approved travel only. Those are different populations. Try explaining this to an imaginary manager who thinks the numbers should be identical. Do not continue until you can make that distinction clearly.

Now exercise D4 G2. A slicer is a visible filter control. Instead of opening a menu inside every column, management can choose a category and immediately see the related PivotTable. Our key example is Approval. When the filter selects Approved, the pivot should exclude Pending values and return two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five rand. When the filter is cleared, all recorded statuses return and the all-status grand total is three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty. A slicer changes the visible population. It does not change the original travel records.

Select the Pivot table or its source range. In Google Sheets, use Data, then Add a slicer. Set the slicer's range to the appropriate data and set the column to Approval. Position it next to your pivot. Choose Approved and check the total. Depending on the layout of your sheet, you may need to position the slicer carefully so it does not cover the table. If the slicer appears to filter the wrong range, inspect the source data range and selected column. This is deliberately different from Excel's PivotTable Analyze, Insert Slicer command.

Try this quick demonstration. First, clear all filters and read the all-status total. Then select Approved and read the approved total. Next select Pending and verify eighty thousand eight hundred and thirty-five rand. Clear the slicer again and confirm you return to the original three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty. The numbers are not changing unpredictably. We are deliberately changing which records are included. Every screenshot and every dashboard that uses a filtered result should make the filter state clear. Otherwise a reader might mistake an Approved-only report for total expenditure.

The exercise asks you to test the behaviour of the pivot when a new trip arrives. Make a copy of the worksheet or workbook first. Add one clearly marked hypothetical approved trip worth one thousand rand. Make sure the pivot data range includes that new row. The approved total would rise from two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five to two hundred and forty-one thousand seven hundred and five. The all-status total would rise to three hundred and twenty-two thousand five hundred and forty. That is only a controlled test, not a real expenditure record. Delete the temporary row and confirm the original totals return before finishing.

In Google Sheets, pivots commonly update as their source values change, but a new row outside the selected source range may not be included. Do not blindly follow the Excel desktop instruction to press Refresh. Instead inspect the Pivot table editor's data range. If it ends at row ninety-one and you inserted a new trip below that limit, extend the range or use a suitably expandable range. Then verify the answer. Remember that filtering rows directly in the source sheet is not the same as applying a pivot filter or slicer. A pivot has its own configuration.

We also need to compare months. The Travel sheet contains a MonthStart helper field in column L: a proper first-of-month date. We can use that field as pivot rows or as a month grouping key. Why not just use the word September? Because September repeats every year. September twenty twenty-five and September twenty twenty-six would become one category if you ignore the year. Proper dates also sort chronologically instead of alphabetically. Make a simple second pivot with MonthStart in Rows and the SUM of TotalCost in Values, then decide whether Approved should be a filter.

Try switching between Approved and all statuses, then test a temporary row on a copy and restore the original source. Your evidence should show the pivot's sum and the filter state. When you finish, the all-status total must once again be three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty rand and the approved total two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five. If not, inspect the new row and data range. Here is your comprehension question. Why does filtering the register itself not guarantee the pivot shows the same filter? Because a pivot has its own source and filter configuration. Pause and answer before moving on.

Now we move to D4 G3: monthly administration performance. This is where people often calculate the right-looking number for the wrong group. Our six monthly cohorts are April, May, June, July, August, and September twenty twenty-six. Correspondence received means an item belongs to the month in which its Received date falls. The Closed share asks how many of those received items are now marked Closed, as at the reporting date. It does not mean how many items happened to close within that month. We will apply the same logic to actions raised in a month and later completed.

Look at the Monthly sheet. Column A contains the first date of each month. Column B is correspondence Received; column C is Closed; D is ClosedShare. Column E is Actions raised; F is Complete; G is CompletionRate; H is ApprovedTravel. The columns are intentionally not all the same type. Counts such as sixteen or ten are whole numbers. Shares such as fifty percent or forty percent are percentages. Travel is currency. Formatting helps readers distinguish these measures, but only formulas define what they mean. Do not put travel amounts into a correspondence count or confuse the two populations.

In Monthly B2, we count correspondence received during April. The date field is Correspondence column B. COUNTIFS lets us apply two conditions to the same date range: on or after the first day of April, and strictly before the first day of May. The first condition includes the start date. The second excludes the next month. Enter the formula shown on screen and press Enter. The April result is sixteen. Then copy the formula down to B7. Each row refers to its own month start in column A, while the source register range stays fixed. Check the total: all six months together contain ninety-six received items.

Let's inspect the dates more carefully. Suppose a letter was received exactly on the first of May. It should not count in April. With a condition of less than the first of May, it is excluded from April but included in May, because May's lower boundary is on or after the first of May. No records are double-counted. By using EDATE of the month start and one, the formula works for months of different lengths. You do not have to remember whether April has thirty days or February has twenty-eight. This half-open date interval is one of the most reliable patterns in reporting.

Now in Monthly C2, count which April-received items are currently marked Closed. That means the same two date tests, plus the condition Correspondence column H equals Closed. The April cohort contains sixteen items, but none of them is currently marked Closed in this fictional dataset. Other months differ. When you copy the formula down, the monthly values are zero, sixteen, zero, sixteen, zero, sixteen. Together they total forty-eight. Notice that you are not filtering by the ClosedDate column. That would answer a different question: how many closure events happened in that month.

A closed count on its own does not show the size of the cohort. We divide Closed by Received. In D2, use IF B2 equals zero, display No records; otherwise divide C2 by B2. Then format as a percentage and copy down to September. For April, zero divided by sixteen is zero percent. For May, sixteen divided by sixteen is one hundred percent. Across the full period, forty-eight closed out of ninety-six received is fifty percent. Be careful: the average of monthly percentages is not always the same as a weighted overall share. Use total closed divided by total received for the overall figure.

Next, open the Actions register. An action has a Raised date in column D, Status in column H, and other columns for due dates and flags. To count actions raised in April, use COUNTIFS on the Raised date range. The two date conditions match the approach we used for correspondence. The difference is the register and source column. There are ten actions raised in each of the six months. That totals sixty. The fact that an action has a deadline in another month does not change when it was originally raised. That distinction is essential if management is measuring how many commitments were created in a particular month.

Monthly F2 should count how many of April's raised actions now have Status Complete. Add a third COUNTIFS criterion for Actions column H equals Complete. In our data, four of the ten April-raised actions are complete. The same four out of ten pattern repeats across the six months. So the complete total is twenty-four. The important phrase is complete among items raised that month, as of our reporting date. We are not counting all completions that occurred during April. If somebody asks a question about actual completion dates, we would need a different measure using CompletedDate in column I.

In Monthly G2, divide the Complete count in F2 by the Actions count in E2, with an IF guard for zero. Four complete divided by ten actions equals forty percent for April. The same percentage appears in each month in this training dataset. Across all months, twenty-four out of sixty is also forty percent. In a real report, we might see different rates across months. The structure matters more than whether this example is flat. Check that a rate is formatted as a percentage and that the denominator is the same raised-month cohort as the numerator.

Now we calculate Monthly H2, approved travel for April. Here the source is Travel. TotalCost is column K, the trip date is B, and Approval is F. SUMIFS adds the TotalCost only when the trip date falls within April and the status is Approved. Unlike COUNTIFS, SUMIFS returns an amount. April's approved travel is sixteen thousand seven hundred and thirty rand. Then copy this formula down to September. Across all six months, the approved travel total must match the Summary sheet's approved expenditure control of two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five rand. That final control check protects us from a wrongly defined date range.

Look at the complete six-month report on screen. Every month has sixteen received correspondence items and ten actions raised, but the Closed count alternates between zero and sixteen. The approved travel amount also varies by month. April has sixteen thousand seven hundred and thirty; May fifty-three thousand two hundred and sixty; June thirty-eight thousand three hundred and fifteen; July thirty-five thousand eight hundred and fifty; August twenty-four thousand five hundred and sixty; and September seventy-one thousand nine hundred and ninety. Add those six travel values and you get two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five. These are answers to verify, not values to type into the calculation cells.

This warning deserves its own demonstration. If you count items received in April, then divide by items closed during April regardless of when they were received, you have mixed two different populations. Your percentage may look plausible but it does not represent the share of April-received items that are now closed. The same applies to actions. Completion status of actions raised in a particular month is different from the number of actions completed during that month. Keep the numerator and denominator within the same cohort when reporting a share. If management wants a flow of closure events, create a separate measure and label it clearly.

Pause here and verify four answers. First, total correspondence received is ninety-six. Second, closed items total forty-eight, giving an overall share of fifty percent. Third, actions raised total sixty and twenty-four are complete, a forty-percent rate. Fourth, the sum of Monthly H2 through H7 is two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five rand. If your figures differ, inspect one month at a time. Do not type the correct totals into the Monthly sheet. Fix the COUNTIFS or SUMIFS logic, and confirm your month-start values are real dates. These source checks will feed our dashboard next.

Welcome to D4 G4, our executive dashboard. A dashboard is not a collection of every chart you know how to create. It is a compact view of measures that answer management questions. We will show correspondence received, closed share, open or overdue action exceptions, and approved travel. Then we will add two charts: a chronological trend and a departmental comparison. The reader should see the reporting date, the measure labels, the period, and the approval basis. If those details are missing, a beautiful dashboard may still be misleading. Think of it as an evidence-based briefing, not decoration.

Our headline values are ninety-six correspondence received, fifty percent of the received cohort closed, thirty-six actions currently flagged Overdue, and two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five rand in approved travel. Each figure comes from a different calculation or register. Received is a count. Closed share is a percentage. Overdue actions is an exception count from the Actions Flag column. Approved travel is a currency total filtered to Approved. We will not calculate overdue actions by guessing from the due dates on today's computer date; the exercise uses a fixed report date and the register's defined flag. This is how we keep the meaning stable.

On the Dashboard sheet, create or use a headline label with a formula that references the correct result. For example, correspondence received can link to the total of Monthly column B, and approved travel can link to Summary B3. The formula should remain live while you are preparing the report. A copy-pasted total without a source link is harder to audit. For closed share, calculate total Closed divided by total Received, not an average of percentages unless the denominator is equal across months and you have verified that reasoning. Every KPI should have a traceable source, and every source should be verified.

A chart should answer a question. A line chart works well for change over ordered time periods. Select the Month and Received columns from Monthly A1 through B7. Use Insert, Chart, and choose a line chart in the Chart editor if Sheets has not chosen one. Title it Correspondence received by month. Check that April through September appear in the correct order, not alphabetically. In this fictional dataset, the count stays at sixteen per month. That flat trend is a valid result. Do not make up fluctuations just to create a more exciting chart.

When we compare approved travel across departments, a horizontal bar chart is usually clearer than a pie chart. Use the approved expenditure values for Executive, Finance, and Operations from the Pivot or a checked Summary table. Name the chart Approved travel by department, South African rand. Executive is eighty-six thousand seven hundred. Finance is seventy-six thousand eight hundred and ten. Operations is seventy-seven thousand one hundred and ninety-five. Label the value axis in rand. Do not mix pending or all-status travel with the Approved-only amounts, or the chart will tell a different story from the headline.

Consider a graph whose label simply says Travel spend. Does it include pending commitments? Approved expenditure? This month only? All six months? We cannot tell. Rename the chart so the population and time period are explicit. Avoid three-dimensional charts that distort bar length. Avoid rainbow colours that imply patterns that are not present. A neutral palette works well for normal values; reserve a contrasting colour for an actual exception, such as an overdue action count. If a chart uses percentages, label the axis as a percentage rather than leaving the unit unexplained.

If you allow dashboard filtering, show the selected status somewhere on screen. An Approved-only total must not be presented as all travel. The report date is thirty September twenty twenty-six and should be visible. A good heading might read Monthly administration performance report, April to September twenty twenty-six. A subheading could state: Travel expenditure includes Approved trips only; closure and completion statuses are measured as at the report date. This looks like a small detail, but it prevents the reader from assuming we counted closure events within each month. Add a clear note when filters are cleared or changed.

Place the title and reporting date at the top. Put four KPI cards beneath it. Leave enough white space so the numbers are readable. Place the line chart on one side and the approved-travel bar chart on the other. Use one or two fonts consistently; do not reduce critical labels to microscopic type merely to fit another widget. Keep the detailed source data on its own tabs rather than printing ninety travel rows on the dashboard page. A dashboard is successful when someone can understand the key message quickly, and then trace the figures when they ask for evidence.

For the handover exercise, review the sheet in print preview. In Google Sheets, use File, Print. Select the current sheet, choose landscape orientation, and adjust scaling carefully so the dashboard fits on one page without shrinking the labels too far. Export a PDF if required. Check it before sharing: are the heading, reporting date, full charts, axis labels, KPI numbers and comments visible? Do not cut off the last column or hide a chart title. Printability is not only an aesthetic requirement. A poorly exported report can change what management thinks it is seeing.

Before we move to reconciliation, take one headline value, such as approved travel of two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five. Explain where it came from. In the Dashboard, follow the link to Summary B3. Then point to the Pivot's Approved column and the six-month approved travel total. The amounts agree because they use the same approval category and full reporting period. Repeat with the ninety-six received correspondence count. If you cannot trace a KPI, it is not ready to present. Pause here and check the dashboard against the source worksheet, not merely against the expected answer.

Now D4 G5. Reconciliation is a check between independently calculated summaries for the same population, period and measure. It is not enough for a pivot to look right or a chart to be colourful. We want proof that all six monthly approved travel amounts add up to the approved total from Summary. The total from Monthly H2 through H7 must be two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five. Summary B3 contains the same approved-spending figure. Subtract one from the other. The correct difference is zero. That simple check is your permission to trust the result, not a license to ignore source problems.

What does a zero difference tell us? It means the six-month approved-travel total reconciles to the approved-travel control. That is useful evidence. But it does not prove every possible field in the workbook is correct. A duplicated trip could affect both calculations in the same way. We still need source integrity checks. Think of reconciliation as one layer of quality assurance. In this exercise, the control result is two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five minus two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five, which equals zero rand. Put that calculation on Notes and label it clearly.

Here is a misleading comparison. Suppose your PivotTable includes all travel and shows three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty, while Monthly sums only approved travel and shows two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five. The difference is eighty thousand eight hundred and thirty-five. Is that an error? No. It is exactly the pending travel amount. You have compared two different populations. The remedy is to filter the pivot to Approved, or compare all-status totals on both sides. Before explaining a variance to management, establish that you are using matching filters and dates.

Reconcile the non-financial registers too. Six monthly Received counts must total ninety-six correspondence items. Six monthly Actions counts must total sixty. If you see fewer than ninety-six correspondence records in the monthly table, perhaps one date is stored as text or your COUNTIFS range stops before the last row. If the total rises above ninety-six, check whether a month boundary overlaps another month, or whether duplicate source IDs exist. A final report needs these checks because an incorrect count can distort both the headline and the percentage derived from it.

Management commentary should have three parts: one measured finding, one proposed action, and one limitation. A finding is something we can point to in the data. For example, thirty-six of sixty actions have the Overdue flag. That is sixty percent, and it warrants attention. A proposed action could be for action owners to review deadlines and update statuses. A limitation would be that this register alone does not explain why the actions became overdue. It might be staffing, dependencies, delayed decisions, or something else, but we have not proved the cause. Do not turn a hypothesis into a factual conclusion.

Here is an example you can adapt. First sentence: As at the thirtieth of September twenty twenty-six, thirty-six of sixty actions were flagged overdue in the register. Second sentence: Management should ask the relevant action owners to review those records and confirm updated target dates or completion evidence. Third sentence: The register identifies the current flags but does not establish the underlying reasons for delay. Notice the wording. We state what is measured and recommend a next step. We do not accuse anybody of poor performance or invent facts that the spreadsheet cannot support. Type your own comment into the Dashboard area designated for management notes.

Before you submit, check the whole workbook. The pivot grand total is three hundred and twenty-one thousand five hundred and forty rand. The Approved filter gives two hundred and forty thousand seven hundred and five. Monthly Received totals ninety-six, Closed totals forty-eight, Actions totals sixty and Complete totals twenty-four. Approved monthly travel adds to the approved total with a difference of zero. The dashboard should label the reporting date and filter basis. Both charts should have correct categories, numbers and units. Restore every temporary source change and clear or document any slicers. Save your own workbook, not over the facilitator's answer copy.

Now it is your turn to produce the administration brief. In your own Day Four workbook, build the department-by-approval pivot and verify its totals. Demonstrate an Approval slicer and restore the all-status view. Calculate all six months in Monthly using date-based COUNTIFS and SUMIFS. Add four trusted KPI values to the Dashboard. Insert one chronological line chart and one approved-spending bar chart. Add a reconciliation check and three evidence-based management sentences. Save your file with your learner identifier, and export a readable one-page dashboard PDF. Do not look at the answer sheet until you have attempted every stage.

Let's finish with five quick questions. Number one: when would you use SUM rather than COUNT in a pivot? Number two: why does selecting Approved produce a smaller total than all statuses? Number three: what is the difference between a received-month cohort share and a count of closures during that month? Number four: why is a line chart appropriate for six ordered months? Number five: what must you do when a reconciliation difference is not zero? Pause after each question and explain the answer in your own words. You should be able to answer without guessing, and you should be able to find supporting evidence in the workbook.

Here are the answers. Use SUM when the question concerns a numeric amount, such as travel expenditure. A slicer changes which records are included, so Approved and all-status totals are different populations. A received-month cohort share measures the status of items originally received in that month, while closure events measure a different date. A line chart shows an ordered trend through time. And a non-zero reconciliation difference means stop, compare periods and filters, inspect the source and fix the calculation before publishing. Congratulations on finishing Day Four. Save and check your work, then prepare for the final integration activities. DotPy: the dot that matters.
